title: What testers hit in talk's side panel, and 21 proposals for a better one
footer: Private copy of talk with a silent voice, 25 November 2026. Testers were Claude agents in role.

screens.label: What this is
screens.html:
What this report is about

Talk is the call page where you speak or type with a Claude Code session. The big area on the left is the stage, where boards such as tables and diagrams appear. The narrow column on the right is the side panel: the conversation, the player, the text box and the settings. This report is about the side panel only.

14 testers used real calls on a private copy of talk: the same code, run on its own so no real call was touched. Each tester was a Claude agent playing a person, not told what was being tested. Another agent answered each call the way a real session does. Then 11 designer agents drew new panels, and 11 new tester agents, not the first 14, compared each drawing with today's panel.

14testers used the page, 5 to 11 messages each
99problems held up, of 111 reported. Three checker agents tried to disprove each one against the code and the screenshots.
21proposals, each drawn on a laptop screen and a phone
11fresh testers voted on every proposal

steps.title: Testers used talk's side panel, and designers proposed 21 better ones
text: Nothing was built or changed. First come the words this report uses, then the problems the testers hit, the proposals in rank order, and one decision for you.

screens.label: Words used
screens.html:
Word
What it means here
Talk
the call page where you speak or type with a Claude Code session, the Claude assistant working on your computer.
Agent
a separate Claude worker given one task. Testers, checkers, designers, reviewers and judges here are all agents.
Reviewer
an agent that checked each proposal's build plan against talk's code and fixed its drawing.
Second page
a long page with every finding, vote and build plan, linked on the last slide.
Call
one conversation, in its own browser tab. You can have several open.
Stage
the big area on the left that shows boards: tables, diagrams, code.
Side panel
the narrow column on the right. It is what this report is about.
Answer
what Claude says back. It is read aloud and the word being said is lit.
Turn
one message of yours and the answer to it.
Fold
an answer shown as one cut-off line until you press Show text.
Chip
a small button under an answer that names a board, such as Key points.
Following the voice
the stage shows the board the voice is talking about.
Queue
an answer waiting to play after the current one ends.
Live mode
hands-free talking: the page listens and sends when you pause.
Player
the play, pause, back and speed controls.
Server
the program on your computer that runs the calls.
Screen reader
software that reads the page aloud to a blind person.

steps.title: These words mean one thing each in this report
text: The proposals use them freely. Button labels on the page are quoted as they appear.

steps.title: Every tester scored the page between 5.5 and 7.5 out of 10
text: Each tester had a different habit: a phone, a TV across the room, keyboard only, a screen reader, Greek, three calls at once. The score is the tester's own, out of 10, for the whole page. The testers are agents, not people, so treat their scores and votes as a strong hint, not proof. Talk normally reads answers aloud and turns your speech into text. In this test the voice was silent and speech-to-text was off, so testers typed and read.

steps.title: The proposals are ranked by how much they help your daily use
text: Three judge agents ranked all 21: one for your daily use with several calls, one for value per day of work, one for the strength of the evidence. A fourth merged their lists. Preferred counts the 11 new testers who chose it over today. Score is their average from 1 to 5, where 3 means the same as today. Work is small under a day, medium one to three days, large more.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 1. The Calls button shows the most urgent state of your other calls
text: Today: With several calls open you cannot tell which one is ready, working or waiting for you, and the browser tab name never changes.

Proposed: One Calls button shows the most urgent state and a count of calls that need you. It opens a list that sorts calls by need and names each state in words. The browser tab name shows the state too.
Votes: 8 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 3 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.3 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The reviewer found that the plan fits the existing code, so the risk is low.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 2. Every message you send shows where it stands and can be taken back
text: Today: After you press Send you get no sign of what happened, and an old answer can start speaking over your correction.
Proposed: Under each message one line says Sent, Claude has it, Answered, Replaced or Taken back, with a wait counter. You can take a message back, and a replaced answer does not speak.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4.1 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that replacing a turn needs new work on the server. Taking a message back already works today.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 3. The wait becomes a card with its own clock, its steps and a way out
text: Today: After Send you see one faint line, and after 180 seconds a warning that tells you to check the terminal.
Proposed: A card under your message counts the wait and shows four steps: Sent, Picked up, Working and Answer. It offers Cancel and Send again.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that cancelling a message Claude already started on is new work on the server. The reviewer also found the time limits in the plan were wrong.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 4. Every message gets a visible life, with a counted wait and a way out
text: Today: When you correct a question while Claude works, the old answer still arrives and plays over the new one, and the warning after a long wait offers no action.
Proposed: Under each message one line says where it is, such as Claude has it or Replaced. The wait is counted, and you can skip an answer in the queue.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4.1 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. This is for the page only. The main risk is that cancelling or replacing a turn needs extra work on the server.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 5. A Now card holds the whole current turn above a list of older answers
text: Today: Every answer is one cut-off line, and the player sits far from the answer it controls.
Proposed: One card shows the current question, the full answer with the lit word, board chips and the player. Earlier answers are rows under it.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4.3 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.

Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that it reverses the documented rule that every answer folds to one line, and the reviewer found the plan wrongly said cancelling needed no server work.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 6. A welcome-back card shows what you missed and plays it in one press
text: Today: A call left open for hours looks the same when you return, with no sign of what is new.
Proposed: After a long absence a card says how long you were away and how many answers, boards and minutes of audio are new. You press Play the new or Read them.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4.2 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that automatic playback must not take over following the voice.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 7. The conversation becomes a searchable list of answers with titles
text: Today: Each answer is cut to one grey line, so finding an older answer costs one press per answer.
Proposed: Every exchange is one row in the same columns: time, your question, a one-line summary, a board button and a play button. A search box and an Expand all button help you find one.
Votes: 9 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 1 saw no difference, 1 preferred today. Average 3.8 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that it breaks the documented rule that every answer folds to one line.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 8. The side panel becomes a list of turns with the newest answer open
text: Today: The side panel is a plain log, so nothing says which board belongs to which answer, and each older answer needs a press to read.
Proposed: Each of your questions becomes the heading of its turn, with its answer, boards and wait under it. The newest turn is open and older ones fold under their question, with a search box.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.8 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that it breaks the documented rule that every answer folds to one line, so that rule must change too.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 9. The side panel says its state in words and has one live status line
text: Today: A person who cannot watch the side panel learns nothing when Claude starts, works, stalls or answers.
Proposed: One line under the title names the state in words and is read aloud by a screen reader. The conversation becomes a list with a heading for each answer.
Votes: 10 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 1 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.8 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.

Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that announcing too much is worse than silence, and the reviewer found the grey line above the text box, where Claude is working… appears, already shows about twelve other messages.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 10. The side panel becomes a thread of titled turns with one control area
text: Today: Frequent controls such as speed and Live mode are hidden in settings, and answers are folded one-line entries.

Proposed: The panel has a header with a state line, a thread of turns with the newest open, and a bottom area for the player, following the voice and the choice of how you talk: Type, Talk or Live mode.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 4 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that it bundles many other proposals into one change.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 11. A line above the text box counts the wait and offers cancel, resend or skip
text: Today: A message sent while Claude works joins the open turn, and the long wait ends in a warning about the terminal.
Proposed: A line above the text box shows the step, a clock and the buttons Cancel, Send again, Ask for status or Skip. Your draft is kept.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.5 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that the reviewer found the plan was wrong about how a new message joins an open turn, so the server work is bigger.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 12. A button row under the player names the answer that plays
text: Today: Speed is only in settings, and nothing says which answer the Play button and the Space key act on.
Proposed: One row names the answer and the sentence now playing. It holds Previous, Next, speed and following the voice, plus a progress bar with marks for sentences.
Votes: 10 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 1 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.9 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that the Space key would act on the answer being played, which changes what it does today.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 13. One state area under the title shows the call state and other calls in words
text: Today: The state is spread over the bottom line, a chip, a small label and dots, and the browser tab name never changes.
Proposed: An area under the title shows a state word, one detail, a clock and the actions that fit. The browser tab name and border show the state from another tab.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.6 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that the reviewer found the plan names several functions that do not exist.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 14. The side panel becomes a calm list of titled answers with one now line
text: Today: At rest the side panel is a log with message bubbles, floating chips and one-line answers.
Proposed: A one-row header has icon buttons. The conversation is a list of titled items, and one line says what plays and what to do.
Votes: 11 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 0 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.9 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that it overlaps other proposals and breaks the documented rule that every answer folds to one line.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 15. One text box area shows how you talk and what the microphone hears
text: Today: The way you talk (typing, press to talk or Live mode) is hidden in settings, and a dead microphone looks the same as a quiet room.
Proposed: A visible Type, Talk and Live switch sits by the text box, with a sign that says it is your turn to speak. Your draft is never lost.
Votes: 10 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 1 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.8 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that the Live part makes the bottom of the side panel taller, and the reviewer found the plan names the wrong function for setting the mode.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 16. On a phone the side panel becomes a panel that slides up from the bottom
text: Today: On a phone with a board shown, the side panel gets 38 percent of the screen height. That leaves about 150 pixels, so you see one cut-off line.
Proposed: The panel slides up from the bottom and has three heights. Its controls sit under the thumb, and the newest answer shows its full text.
Votes: 10 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 1 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.5 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that showing the newest answer in full breaks the documented rule that every answer folds to one line.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 17. A permanent column lists every call and its state beside the stage
text: Today: Other calls sit behind a button and a popup, so each switch costs a press and a guess.
Proposed: A column beside the stage lists every call with its state and age, sorted by need. A button jumps to the first call that needs you.
Votes: 3 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 6 saw no difference, 2 preferred today. Average 3 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that the column takes 272 of the 1440 pixels of a laptop screen's width, which is the width the stage needs most.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 18. Settings move to a plain list and the empty first screen gets starter questions
text: Today: The settings popup holds eleven controls in jargon and does not fit on short windows.
Proposed: Settings become a panel of labelled rows in plain words. Talk mode and speed sit beside the controls, and an empty call offers starter questions.
Votes: 8 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 3 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.2 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that a new Type mode needs the microphone to be reliably off.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 19. Settings and shortcuts open in panels that keyboard users reach quickly
text: Today: A keyboard user needs about 30 presses of the Tab key to reach Voice speed, because the cursor never enters the settings popup.
Proposed: Settings open in a panel where the keyboard cursor moves in, stays inside and returns when you close it. A list of every shortcut sits beside its button.
Votes: 3 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 7 saw no difference, 1 preferred today. Average 3.1 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that some key combinations clash with the browser or the system.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 20. A top bar says in words and sounds what the call is doing
text: Today: Someone who is not looking at the screen gets no word or sound when Claude starts, works or answers.
Proposed: A bar at the top of the side panel names one of five states in words, short sounds mark each change, and spoken commands control playback.
Votes: 8 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 2 saw no difference, 1 preferred today. Average 3.6 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.
Work: Large work, more than three days. The main risk is that browsers block sound until the person has pressed something, and spoken commands already exist in part.

screens.source: Left: today's panel. Right: the proposal's mock-up, same conversation where possible.

steps.title: 21. TV mode becomes a setting that is offered and easy to find
text: Today: TV mode, which makes everything larger, is only in settings, and a TV opens the page at the normal desktop size.
Proposed: A button in the header switches between Desk and TV, and a link can open a call in TV size. One scale setting enlarges everything.
Votes: 3 of 11 testers preferred it to today, 8 saw no difference, 0 preferred today. Average 3.2 out of 5, where 3 means the same as today.

Work: Medium work, one to three days. The main risk is that the page cannot tell a TV from a monitor, and the reviewer found the plan assumed a third, phone, screen mode, when the code has only Desk and TV.

steps.title: Five steps take the best of each family of proposals
text: Several proposals solve the same problem in different ways. These steps combine the best of each. In all they are at least seven days of Claude's work, more for step 3, plus a day for the quick fixes on the next slide. Proposals #10, #14, #17, #18 and #21 are in no step: they repeat a better-ranked proposal or did not beat today in the votes.

screens.label: Quick fixes
screens.html:
Before

Small defects in the panel that need no design decision:

• Today the status lines in the conversation stretch into blank gaps hundreds of pixels tall, and the fix keeps them one line high.

• Today a hint, the small text that appears over a button, opens upward onto the player time and stays, and the fix shows it only on keyboard focus or after a short delay.

• Today the hint for the Expand button covers the Copy button on the stage header, and the fix opens it away from the stage edge.

• Today the warning after 180 seconds tells you to check the terminal, and the fix says what to do in plain words and adds Send again and Copy question buttons.

• Today the line Claude is working shows no clock, and the fix shows the seconds counted from when you pressed Send.

• Today on a short screen the End call button is hidden below the visible part of the settings popup, and the fix makes it reachable.

• Today the step arrows on a board have no name for a screen reader and All shown looks like a label, and the fix names the arrows and makes All shown look like a button.

After

Each is a small change in the panel's own code, under a day for all of them together. The stage defects the testers hit are listed on the second page.

The second page has every finding, every proposal in full with its build plan, and every vote.

steps.title: 7 small panel defects can be fixed without any design decision
text: They come from the same test. The largest is the status notes that stretch into blank gaps. The second page holds everything else: all findings, the rejected ones, each proposal's build plan and the testers' own words.

screens.label: Decision
screens.html:
Today

The panel stays as it is. The problems in this report stay too.

Yes

Claude builds the quick fixes first, then steps 1 to 5 in order. Step 2 covers the page only; the server part that cancels a turn is a later step of its own. Each step goes into claude-annotate, your own tools repository where this report lives, on its own, so you can try it on a real call before the next one starts.

No

Nothing changes. This report and its proposals stay in the claude-annotate repository for later.

steps.title: Decide whether Claude builds the quick fixes and the five steps
text: To answer, write build the talk panel steps in this session's chat, or name the ones you want, such as quick fixes and steps 1 and 2, or write no. A step can be taken back by reverting its change. Every finding, vote and build plan is on the second page.
